Newborn silvery mole-rats emerge from the birth canal at a remarkably modest body mass for a bathyergid rodent; field studies report that neonates typically weigh approximately 9 grams [Wwb = approximately 9 grams] at parturition. This altricial birth mass reflects the species' adaptation to a subterranean lifestyle, where energy conservation during gestation is paramount. The pups are entirely dependent on maternal care during the initial weeks, with milk ingestion onset occurring shortly after the birth event. As the suckling juvenile progresses, its body mass increases steadily until the weaning process begins. The nutritional independence of these young animals is achieved when they have reached a wet weight at weaning of roughly 80 grams [Wwx = roughly 80 grams], a threshold that typically coincides with the emergence of foraging behavior within the natal tunnel system. The transition from milk dependence to a solid food diet, primarily composed of geophytes and underground storage organs, marks a critical period in juvenile development, with the weaned juvenile subsequently beginning to explore the colony's extensive burrow network.

Under the thermoneutral conditions typical of this species' deep-soil burrows, maintained at 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C], female silvery mole-rats exhibit a remarkably constrained maximum reproductive rate. The per-litter output consists of two pups per birth event [N_R_i = two pups per birth event], a modest litter size that is consistent with the species' slow life-history strategy. Breeding females are capable of producing slightly more than one such litter over the course of a year, with the frequency of reproductive events reaching approximately 1.2 litters annually [F_R_i = approximately 1.2 litters annually]. This limited reproductive output, when combined with the small litter size, yields a low annual recruitment rate, a pattern that is typical of many solitary or paucispecific bathyergids that inhabit unpredictable, arid environments where the energetic costs of burrow excavation and thermoregulation are substantial. The gestation period itself lasts for 88 days [tg = 88 days] under the aforementioned stable thermal regime of 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C], a relatively prolonged intrauterine development that is likely linked to the altricial state of the offspring at birth.

The basal metabolic rate of the silvery mole-rat, measured as the maximum resting oxygen consumption under controlled laboratory conditions, reaches approximately 154 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = approximately 154 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a temperature of 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C]. This value, recorded at the species' preferred ambient temperature of 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C], is notably low when compared to other rodents of similar body size, reflecting the energetic economy enforced by life in an underground ecotope. The ultimate wet weight, representing the asymptotic adult body mass attained by fully grown individuals, is approximately 223 grams [Wwi = approximately 223 grams]. This considerable adult mass is achieved through a prolonged growth trajectory that extends well beyond the weaning stage. The low resting metabolism is a key adaptation for surviving the challenges of hypoxia and hypercapnia that characterize deep burrow atmospheres, allowing the species to maintain somatic function on a reduced energetic budget while foraging for widely dispersed underground food resources.

The developmental trajectory of female silvery mole-rats includes a substantial delay in reaching the pubertal state, with the time since birth at puberty for females documented at 365 days since birth [tp = 365 days since birth] when the colony is maintained at a stable ambient temperature of 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C]. This lengthy period of immaturity, lasting approximately one full year from the birth event, represents a substantial investment in somatic growth and behavioral maturation before the onset of reproductive capability. During this time, the juvenile and subsequently sub-adult female remains within the natal burrow system, contributing to colony maintenance and tunnel defense. The time since birth at weaning, conversely, occurs much earlier in development, at approximately 65 days post-partum [tx = approximately 65 days post-partum], marking the transition to nutritional independence at a temperature of 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C]. The extended gap between tx and tp highlights a prolonged juvenile phase that is characteristic of slow-living mammals, during which the growing individual must accumulate sufficient body reserves and explore its subterranean environment before attempting to reproduce.

Maximum documented longevity in the silvery mole-rat, recorded under stable captive conditions at a temperature of 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C], is reported to be roughly 13.5 years [am = roughly 13.5 years], an exceptional lifespan for a rodent of this body mass. This extraordinary longevity, far exceeding that of most small mammals, is intimately linked to the species' extremely low basal metabolic rate and its delayed reproductive schedule. The extended lifespan provides ample opportunity for a female to offset her delayed pubertal onset and low annual fecundity through repeated breeding attempts across many years. Comparative studies among African mole-rats suggest that such extended lifespans are correlated with the degree of sociality and the stability of the underground environment, with the silvery mole-rat, despite being predominantly solitary, exhibiting a lifespan that rivals that of the eusocial naked mole-rat. The geriatric phase of life is marked by a gradual decline in locomotor activity and foraging efficiency, though senile mortality typically occurs without a prolonged period of physiological deterioration under favorable husbandry conditions.
